UC Berkeley Major Migration

One page, three passes over the same student flows, in rising order of depth: a flow diagram tracing each entering class from intended major to declared major to degree (including no degree at all); a role grid showing the measured role each department plays, cohort by cohort; and a department scatter plot placing every department by how much of its intenders’ traffic it keeps and how much of its population it imports — with time, admit rates, and demographics layered on. Between the first and the rest sits a plain reading of the same flows, one intended department at a time. The same head counts are also drawn as an exchange network — the trading pattern the role grid measures — with a link to the full department-grain graph.

UC Berkeley major migration · intended → declared → degree

Intended, Declared, Degree

Entering students traced through three stages — what they intended on the application, what they declared, and the division that finally granted their degree, including the students who left with no degree at all, so the right-hand edge is a full partition of the entering cohort. Units switches between records — one row per student per major, which is what adds up and what the corridors are measured in — and distinct students, which is what you probably mean by “how many people”. The two differ by 1.62×, unevenly, so it is worth looking at both. Hover a band for its year-by-year history and the department flows inside it; click a stage-1 or stage-3 node to trace its students through all three stages; drag a node up or down to reorder its column.

One department at a time

The views around this one are cumulative — every department at once. This is the same data read the plainest way there is: pick an intended major and see where those students declared, where they graduated, and the joint of the two.

Where they declared

Where they graduated

Each row counts students once. Rows do not sum to the total and are not meant to: a student who finished two majors is counted in both. The five figures at the top do partition — intended = finished in it + finished only elsewhere + never finished.

Declared, then graduated

The joint of the two lists above: rows are the departments these students declared, columns the departments whose degree they finished with. Shading is log-scaled, so each doubling of a cell steps the color by about the same amount.

The joint of the two lists above: rows are declared departments, columns are the degrees those same students finished in. Each cell is a head count; rows and columns are ranked by size but deliberately carry no totals, since a total would count double majors twice. Read the off-diagonal carefully — where a pair is roughly symmetric, as Mathematics and EECS-CDSS are at 645 and 617 across the freshman decade, the cell is mostly joint majors, not students who switched. Asymmetry is what marks a one-way corridor.

The exchange network

The flow diagram above reads left to right; this is the same head-count layer drawn as a graph, so the structure of the exchange is visible: which units trade students with which, in both directions at once. Every figure is distinct students — the identical numbers to the flow diagram, re-projected. The role grid below types departments by exactly this exchange pattern; here is the pattern itself, at division grain.

Entrants
Transition
Layout
≥ 0

Every printed figure keeps one grain. Intended-stage node totals are distinct students; declared- and degree-stage figures count declared majors and degree outcomes — a double major contributes one to each unit they declared, which is a fact about double majors, not an error. Ties, rings and percentages are all measured against the node side they touch, the same convention as the ribbons in the flow diagram, so no share can exceed 100%. Where a pair of opposite ties is roughly symmetric, the corridor is mostly joint majors; asymmetry is what marks a genuine one-way movement. Click any node or legend entry to isolate its exchanges; click the background to release.

UC Berkeley major migration · structural roles, measured

Department Migration Roles

Departments play measurable roles in the migration system — some keep their intenders, some are built on arrivals, some feed one corridor. Start with the role grid just below: which role each department plays, cohort by cohort, with the roles found by clustering the flow data itself. Then move to the department scatter plot beneath it — every department placed by how much of its intenders’ traffic it keeps (→ right) and how much of its population is imported (↑ up), with each cohort’s trail, decade-long paths, and admit rates drawn as rings around the dots.

Right = of everyone who intended it, a large share ended there (head count). Up = built on imports (or, on the concentration axis: its leavers funnel into one corridor). Dot area = people. Ring = the admit rate of the department’s college (arc length = the rate). Tail = the previous four cohorts. Hatched = partial data; hollow = recording artifact. Click a dot to pin it — the panel on the right fills with its numbers.
